Slaty finches (Haplospiza rustica) hatched from eggs incubated at 38 °C [T = 38 °C] emerge after a relatively brief developmental period of 13 days [ab = 13 days], a duration that aligns with the altricial life-history strategy typical of many emberizid finches. At the moment of hatching, these altricial nestlings weigh a meager 1.16 grams [Ww0 = 1.16 grams], reflecting the limited yolk reserves available to support early ontogeny before parental provisioning begins. This initial wet weight is among the lowest recorded for Neotropical passerines of comparable adult size, underscoring the intensity of parental care required during the nestling phase. The hatchlings are entirely dependent on their parents for thermoregulation and food delivery during the first several days post-emergence, a period during which the brooding parent maintains the microclimate of the nest at stable temperatures. Field observations confirm that the incubation temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C] is consistently maintained by the attending adult, ensuring optimal conditions for embryonic development and the timely resorption of yolk sacs.

The ontogenetic trajectory from hatching to nutritional independence progresses through several well-defined stages in the Slaty finch. Under the thermal conditions typically experienced during the active season, which hover around 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] for metabolically demanding activities, the nestlings achieve a critical developmental milestone: fledging occurs at 15.5 days after hatching [tx = 15.5 days after hatching], marking the point at which the downy chicks develop sufficient wing feather maturation and flight feather growth to make their first flight achievement and depart the nest. This relatively short fledging period, measured under controlled ambient temperatures approximating 40.2 °C, is characteristic of species that breed in montane environments where the breeding season is constrained by seasonal rainfall patterns. The post-fledging dispersal phase follows almost immediately, with young birds becoming increasingly independent from parental provisioning over the subsequent weeks, though they may still be fed by adults during the initial period after nest departure. This rapid developmental pace is an adaptive response to the ephemeral availability of insect prey in their highland habitats.

Sexual maturation in the Slaty finch is a protracted process relative to its rapid early development. The attainment of sexual maturity occurs 52.5 days after hatching [tp = 52.5 days after hatching] when maintained under the typical thermal environment of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] that characterizes their active foraging bouts, a timeline that allows for the completion of somatic growth and the accumulation of sufficient body condition before the onset of gonadal swelling and gametogenesis onset. This age at puberty, measured from the time of hatching under the same temperature regime, precedes the first successful breeding event by a considerable margin, as young birds require additional time to establish territories and acquire the foraging skills necessary to support the energetic demands of reproduction. The delay between puberty and first reproduction reflects the challenges faced by juveniles in securing a high-quality territory in the competitive social environment of their cloud forest habitat. The first-year birds typically exhibit lower reproductive success than experienced adults, a pattern commonly observed in long-lived passerine species.

The female Slaty finch attains an ultimate adult body mass of 15.5 grams [Wwi = 15.5 grams], a size that is reached gradually through the juvenile and sub-adult stages following the initial rapid weight gain from the 1.16 grams [Ww0 = 1.16 grams] hatchling mass. This maximum recorded body mass in females, documented from museum specimen series and field measurements, represents the plateau at which reproductive activity becomes viable. First reproduction in the wild typically occurs at 343 days after hatching [tR = 343 days after hatching] under the warm ambient conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] that prevail during the breeding season, indicating that females typically defer their first clutch laying until their second calendar year. This deferred breeding strategy is common among small Neotropical passerines and is likely linked to the time required to attain the 15.5 grams necessary to sustain the energetic costs of egg formation and incubation. The females produce a limited annual reproductive output, with clutches consisting of 3 to 4 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 3 to 4 eggs per clutch] and typically just one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year], a pattern that emphasizes offspring quality over quantity.

Lifespan data for the Slaty finch indicate a maximum longevity of approximately 8.3 years [am = approximately 8.3 years] when measured under the thermal conditions of their active metabolic state at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], based on field records from long-term banding studies in the Andes. This lifespan is comparatively extended for a seed-eating finch of its size and aligns with the slow life-history pace implied by the single annual clutch. The basal metabolic rate of this species, determined through respirometry trials at a body temperature of 40.2 °C, is 25.45 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 25.45 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that reflects the modest energetic demands of a bird inhabiting cool, high-altitude cloud forests where thermoregulatory costs are elevated at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This resting metabolic rate is consistent with predictions based on body mass for Neotropical passerines, though slightly lower than expected for a temperate-zone finch of equivalent size, suggesting a potential metabolic adaptation to the relatively stable thermal environment of the tropical montane zone. The combination of deferred reproduction, modest clutch size, and extended lifespan positions the Slaty finch as a classic K-selected strategist within its ecological community.
